title: Gospel, Taizé and worship songs
hookLine: from Black gospel choirs to Taizé's repeated chants to modern worship bands

lines: A CHOIR AND A HAMMOND ORGAN.
cards: Three rooms, one Sunday. In the first, a choir in bright robes sways, a Hammond organ growls, and a soloist holds one note until the whole church is on its feet.

In the second, a church in a French village, young people from many countries sit on the floor in candlelight, singing one short phrase over and over, quieter each time, until it feels like breathing.

In the third, a converted warehouse, the lights go low, a drummer counts in, and a band plays while people raise their hands. Three sounds, and people in all three rooms might use the same word for it: prayer.

teach.b: Gospel means good news, and it names a music born in Black churches in America. It grew out of the spirituals, the blues and the energy of Pentecostal worship. The man often called its father is Thomas A.
Dorsey, a Chicago blues pianist. His wife died giving birth, and their baby son soon after.

teach.h: DORSEY: PRECIOUS LORD, OUT OF GRIEF.
teach.b: In that grief, he sat down at a piano and wrote Take My Hand, Precious Lord. Mahalia Jackson sang it across the world, and it was sung at Martin Luther King Junior's funeral.

Gospel music often comes out of the hardest places. Taizé is something else: a small community of brothers in a village in France, begun by Brother Roger, its members from Protestant and Catholic churches.
Young people come to spend a week there.

teach.h: TAIZÉ: ONE LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
teach.b: The songs are short, one line of scripture or prayer sung again and again, in Latin or in many languages. The hope is that somewhere in the repeats, singers stop thinking about the words and start praying them.
Then modern worship music: guitars, drums, songs sung straight to God, now familiar in churches around the world.
Not every church uses instruments. Orthodox worship is traditionally sung without them, and some Protestant churches, like the Churches of Christ, sing unaccompanied on purpose.

teach.h: LET EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH.
teach.b: Others use every instrument they can find, because Psalm 150 says, in the King James Bible: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Christians argue about music, sometimes loudly.
But a choir, a chant and a band can all carry the same prayer.

how: Christians sing in many styles: gospel choirs in many Black churches, Taizé chants at prayer services across denominations, contemporary worship bands in many Protestant churches, and unaccompanied chant in Orthodox and some Protestant churches.

o: sit down at the piano and write a song to God.
go back to playing only the blues.
games.why: out of that grief he wrote Take My Hand, Precious Lord, which Mahalia Jackson carried around the world.

practice: In your mind, listen to the style of church music that feels least like you: the gospel choir, the quiet chant, the loud band, the old organ.
Imagine yourself in that room, next to someone for whom this is exactly how prayer sounds, and let yourself be curious rather than critical. If you pray, pray alongside them in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Gospel. Good news, and a music born in Black churches in America, where grief and joy share one song.

orig.note: Greek: good news. English gospel comes from the Old English for good news, gōdspel.
